questions.question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Ace in the hole

options.text: To create noisy disturbances so that competitors are unable to work.
A major advantage that one keeps hidden until an ideal time.
To attempt to do the impossible.
To suffer an injury on the lower body.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **A major advantage that one keeps hidden until an ideal time**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **"Ace in the hole"** is an idiomatic expression that originated from poker, specifically stud poker. In stud poker, each player receives some cards face-up and others face-down. The face-down cards are called "hole cards." The "ace" is the highest-ranking card in many card games.
 
• The idiom "Ace in the hole" figuratively refers to a hidden advantage or resource that a person keeps secret until the right moment.
 
• It represents a powerful tool or strategy that can be revealed when needed to gain a significant advantage over others. This advantage is typically withheld or kept in reserve until an opportune time arises, maximizing its impact and effectiveness.

Therefore, the correct meaning of the idiom "Ace in the hole" is:** A major advantage that one keeps hidden until an ideal time**.

Hence, the correct answer is: **Gauge**.

questions.question:
**Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.**

He has been / told many a times to / mind his manners.
questions.solution:
The erroneous part is: **told many a times to**.

• The correct phrase is "many times" without the indefinite article **"a"**.
 
• The phrase "many a" is used to emphasize singularity or uniqueness, as in "many a man" or "many a time."
 
• However, when discussing repetition or frequency, the correct phrase is simply "many times."

The corrected sentence would be: *He has been told **many times** to mind his manners.*

• The idiom "Over and above" is used to indicate something that is in addition to what has already been mentioned or expected.
 
• It suggests an extra or additional element that goes beyond what is required or anticipated. It implies going the extra mile or exceeding expectations.
 
• For example, if someone is given a task to complete within a specific timeframe, and they complete it ahead of schedule and also provide additional supplementary information, it can be said that they have gone "over and above" the initial requirements. questions.question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.

Gloria said, “His relatives are landing tomorrow.”

options.text: Gloria said that his relatives are landing the next day.
Gloria said that his relatives were landing the previous day.
Gloria said that his relatives were landing the next day.
Gloria said that his relatives have been landing the next day.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Gloria said that his relatives were landing the next day**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The sentence in the Direct Speech is in **Present Continuous Tense**. Therefore, the sentence in the Indirect Speech should be in **Past Continuous Tense**.
 
• Present Continuous **(Subject + is/am/are + V1 +ing + Object)** should be converted into Past Continuous **(Subject + was/were + V1 + ing + Object)**.
 
• For example:
 
 
• He said, “I am checking the assignment.” (Direct Speech)
 
• He said that he was checking the assignment. (Indirect Speech)
 
 
 
• The following things in the sentence should change when changed from Direct speech to Indirect Speech:
 
 
• 'said' is changed into 'said that'.
 
• 'tomorrow' is changed into 'the next day'.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Gloria said that his relatives were landing the next day**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The phrase "along with" is the most appropriate choice to fill the blank in the given sentence. Let's analyze the grammatical reasons for this choice:
 
 
• **"off in": **This option does not fit the context of the sentence. The phrase "off in" implies movement away or separation from a specific location, which does not align with the intended meaning of the sentence.
 
• **"within": **This option is not suitable because it implies being inside or contained within something. It does not convey the sense of walking out of a store or ordering online, as indicated in the sentence.
 
• **"up in": **This option is not the correct choice as it does not convey the intended meaning. The phrase "up in" typically implies a location or position higher or above something, which does not fit the context of walking out of a store or ordering online.
 
• **"along with": **This is the correct option as it conveys the meaning of accompanying or together with something. In the given sentence, it effectively communicates the idea that the good feeling is experienced when walking out of a store or ordering online, along with the new shade of lipstick or killer pair of boots.
 
 
 
• In summary, "along with" is the most appropriate choice grammatically and contextually because it accurately conveys the notion of accompanying or being together with the new shade of lipstick or killer pair of boots while experiencing the good feeling mentioned in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **along with**.

• **"summed up":** While "summed up" is a valid phrase, it does not accurately convey the intended meaning in the context of the sentence. "Summed up" means to provide a concise summary or conclusion, which is not the same as scientific studies confirming the effectiveness of retail therapy.

• **"sold on":** "Sold on" means to persuade or convince someone to accept or believe something. It does not fit the context of scientific studies confirming the effectiveness of retail therapy.
 
 
 
• In summary, the correct option is "backed up" because it conveys the meaning that more than one scientific study has provided support or evidence for the effectiveness of retail therapy.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **or**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The conjunction **"or"** is the appropriate choice to fill the blank in the given sentence. Let's analyze the grammatical reasons for this choice:

 
 
• **"if": **The conjunction "if" introduces a conditional clause, suggesting a condition or possibility. However, in this sentence, there is no conditional relationship being expressed.
 
• **"and":** The conjunction "and" is used to join two or more elements together. However, in this sentence, using "and" would imply that shopping takes both time and concentration in both scenarios: online and in a favorite store. This doesn't accurately reflect the intended meaning that shopping takes time and concentration in either scenario.
 
• **"or":** This is the correct option as it indicates a choice or alternative between two options. In this sentence, it appropriately conveys that shopping takes time and concentration whether it is being done online or in a favorite store. It presents two possibilities without implying that both are occurring simultaneously.
 
• **"so":** The conjunction "so" is used to indicate a consequence or result. However, in this sentence, there is no cause-and-effect relationship being expressed.
 
 
 
• In summary, the correct option is "or" because it accurately conveys the choice or alternative between shopping online or in a favorite store, indicating that shopping takes time and concentration in either scenario.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **or**.
